title: Classes, constructors and operator overloading
subtitle: Put the data behind a wall and let the methods guard it.

sections.title: Defining a class
sections.body: Members are private by default in a class (public in a struct). Keep data private and offer public methods: the class can then enforce rules (balance never negative) that raw data cannot. Watch the guard in action — the negative deposit is ignored.

choices.text: So the class controls every change and can protect its rules.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Invariants cannot be broken from outside.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — Defining a class
figures.note: Encapsulation: the invalid deposit never changes the balance.

sections.title: Constructors and destructors
sections.body: A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs when an object is created — use it (and the initialiser list) to put the object in a valid state. A destructor ~Name() runs when it is destroyed: close files, free memory. A copy constructor builds a new object from an existing one; if the class owns a raw pointer, copy the pointed data (deep copy), not just the pointer.

choices.text: When the object is destroyed (scope end or delete).

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — object lifetime
figures.note: RAII: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor.

sections.title: this, static and const
sections.body: this is a pointer to the current object. A static member belongs to the class, shared by all objects (an instance counter). A const method promises not to change the object, so it can be called on const objects.

choices.text: Shared by all objects of the class.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — this, static and const
figures.note: this->x is the member; plain x is the parameter.

sections.title: Operator overloading
sections.body: C++ lets a class define what + - == << [] mean for it: Vec operator+(const Vec& o) const makes a + b work on vectors. Rules: you cannot invent new operators or change precedence; :: . .* ?: cannot be overloaded; keep the meaning intuitive. The expression a + b is just sugar for a.operator+(b).

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — a + b
figures.note: The operator is an ordinary method call in disguise.

problems.prompt: Complex(2,3) + Complex(1,−5) with operator+ adding parts. Result?

sections.title: Friends and stream operators
sections.body: A friend function may touch private members. It is how operator<<(ostream&, const T&) is usually written — the left operand is the stream, not your class, so it cannot be a member. Return the stream to allow chaining: cout << a << b.

questions.prompt: Why is operator<< for printing usually a non-member?

choices.text: The left operand is the ostream, not your class.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A member would need your object on the left.

sections.title: Conversions
sections.body: A one-argument constructor is an implicit conversion (mark it explicit to stop surprises). A conversion operator operator double() converts out. Use them sparingly: hidden conversions make code harder to read.
